q: What is Maven used for in a Java project?
o: Only to run the program once it has been built
Building the project and managing its dependencies
Writing the documentation for the whole project
Editing the source code files of the project
e:
Maven is a build tool. You describe the project in one file, `pom.xml` (Project Object Model): its name and version, the libraries it needs (dependencies) and the plugins to use.
With one command (`mvn package`) Maven downloads the libraries, compiles the code, runs the tests and creates the JAR or WAR.
It follows "convention over configuration": source in `src/main/java`, tests in `src/test/java`, output in `target/`. Gradle is a popular alternative.
r: Maven = pom.xml describes the project; commands build it.
fa: Building the project (compile, test, package) and managing dependencies, driven by a `pom.xml` file

q: What do the Maven coordinates `groupId`, `artifactId` and `version` identify?
o: The postal address and contact data of the author
A unique artifact: its group, its name and its version
The server where the project runs in production
The results of the tests of the project's build
e:
Every Maven artifact is identified by GAV: Group, Artifact, Version.
Example: `org.springframework.boot : spring-boot-starter-web : 3.3.0`.
- `groupId`: usually the reverse domain of the organization (`com.acme`).
- `artifactId`: the name of the library or project.
- `version`: the release (`1.4.2`, or `1.5.0-SNAPSHOT` for work in progress).
With these three Maven finds the right file in a repository.
r: GAV = group + artifact + version.
fa: A unique artifact (library or project): who publishes it (group), its name, and which version

q: Which is the correct order of the main Maven default lifecycle phases?
o: package, compile, test, install, verify, deploy
validate, compile, test, package, verify, install
compile, deploy, test, package, install, validate
test, compile, install, clean, package, validate
e:
Maven's default lifecycle runs phases in order, and running a phase also runs all previous ones:
1. validate: check the project is correct.
2. compile: compile `src/main/java`.
3. test: run unit tests.
4. package: create the JAR/WAR.
5. verify: run integration checks.
6. install: copy the artifact to your local repository (`~/.m2`).
7. deploy: upload it to a remote repository.
`clean` belongs to a separate lifecycle: it deletes `target/`.
r: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy.
fa: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy

q: What is the difference between `mvn package` and `mvn install`?
o: There is no difference between them in Maven builds
`package` makes the JAR; `install` also copies it to ~/.m2
`install` deletes the JAR from `target/` after building
`package` uploads the JAR to the internet repository
e:
Both compile, test and package. `mvn package` stops after creating the JAR/WAR in the `target/` folder.
`mvn install` goes further and copies the artifact into the local repository (`~/.m2/repository`), so other projects on your machine can use it as a dependency.
`mvn deploy` goes even further and uploads to a shared remote repository (Nexus, Artifactory) for your team.
A common daily command is `mvn clean install`.
ec:
mvn clean install          # delete target/, build, test, install locally
mvn clean package -DskipTests   # build without running tests
r: package = JAR in target. install = + local repo. deploy = + remote repo.
fa: `package` builds the JAR in `target/`; `install` also copies it into your local Maven repository (`~/.m2`) so other local projects can depend on it

q: What do the Maven dependency scopes `compile`, `provided`, `runtime` and `test` mean?
o: They are the names of branches used in a Git repository
Build and run, build only, run only, and tests only
They define the author and license of each library
They are the version numbers of a Maven release
e:
The scope controls when a dependency is on the classpath:
- `compile` (default): always, and it is packaged.
- `provided`: available at compile time but not packaged, because the server provides it (e.g. the Servlet API in an external Tomcat).
- `runtime`: not needed to compile, needed at execution (e.g. a JDBC driver).
- `test`: only when compiling and running tests (JUnit, Mockito).
r: test = tests only; provided = server gives it; runtime = needed only to run.
fa: `compile`: needed to build and run; `provided`: needed to build but supplied by the runtime; `runtime`: not needed to compile but needed to run; `test`: only for tests

q: What is a transitive dependency?
o: A dependency that changes very often between releases
A library you did not declare, pulled in by another one
A dependency that is only used while running the tests
A library written in another programming language
e:
If your project depends on library A, and A depends on B, Maven also downloads B for you: B is a transitive dependency.
It is convenient, but it can cause version conflicts when two libraries need different versions of C. Maven resolves it with "nearest definition wins": the version closest to your project in the dependency tree.
Inspect the tree with `mvn dependency:tree`; exclude or pin versions with `<exclusions>` or `dependencyManagement`.
r: Transitive = dependencies of your dependencies.
fa: A library you did not declare, pulled in because one of your dependencies needs it

q: What is a `-SNAPSHOT` version in Maven?
o: A stable release that never changes after publishing
A development version that can change over time
A version that cannot be built with Maven or Gradle
A backup copy of the release kept in a repository
e:
A version such as `1.2.0-SNAPSHOT` means "work in progress toward 1.2.0". The artifact with that same version can be replaced many times.
A release version like `1.2.0` should never change once published: anyone who depends on it gets exactly the same bytes.
Good practice: never depend on SNAPSHOTs in production builds, because the build is not reproducible.
r: SNAPSHOT = mutable work in progress; release = fixed forever.
fa: A development version that can change; Maven may re-download it as it is updated, unlike an immutable release

q: What do `<parent>` and `<dependencyManagement>` (BOM) help with in a pom?
o: Naming the project and listing all of its modules
Centralizing versions so modules stay consistent
Running the tests faster using parallel threads
Publishing the project to Git on every build
e:
`<parent>`: your pom inherits configuration from another pom. `spring-boot-starter-parent` sets plugin defaults and dependency versions.
`<dependencyManagement>`: lists versions in one place. Children and dependencies then omit `<version>`. A BOM (Bill of Materials) is a pom that only does this, such as `spring-boot-dependencies`; you import it and get a tested set of compatible versions.
Benefits: fewer conflicts, one place to upgrade, multi-module projects stay aligned.
r: Parent pom or BOM = one place that decides versions.
fa: Centralizing versions so many dependencies and modules stay consistent without repeating version numbers

q: What is the difference between Maven Surefire and Failsafe plugins?
o: They are the same plugin under two different names
Surefire runs unit tests (`*Test`); Failsafe runs `*IT`
Surefire builds Docker images for the application
Failsafe only works on Windows machines and servers
e:
Plugins do the real work in each Maven phase.
- maven-surefire-plugin: runs unit tests during `test` (classes named `*Test`).
- maven-failsafe-plugin: runs integration tests (classes named `*IT`) during `integration-test`, and checks results in `verify`. This separation lets Maven shut down external things (like a test server) before reporting failure.
This split keeps `mvn test` fast.
r: Surefire = unit tests. Failsafe = integration tests.
fa: Surefire runs unit tests in the `test` phase (`*Test`); Failsafe runs integration tests in `integration-test`/`verify` (`*IT`) so a failure does not leave resources half-cleaned

q: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
o: They are the same product with two different names
Git is the version control tool; GitHub hosts repos
GitHub is a text editor that is made for coding
Git only works when it is used together with GitHub
e:
Git is a distributed version control system: it records the history of your files so you can see changes, go back, and work on parallel versions (branches). It runs locally and needs no internet.
GitHub (also GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps) is a service that stores a shared copy of the repository and adds collaboration: pull requests, code review, issues and automated pipelines.
r: Git = tool. GitHub = hosting platform for Git repos.
fa: Git is the version control tool on your computer; GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories and adds pull requests, issues and CI

q: Git has three main areas on your machine. Which list is correct?
o: Working directory, staging area, local repository
Server, client, cache, and the remote repository
Branch, tag, commit, and the local configuration
Backup, restore, delete, and the history logs
e:
1. Working directory: the files you see and edit.
2. Staging area (index): a waiting room where you choose what goes into the next commit (`git add`).
3. Local repository: the permanent history of commits (`git commit`).
Then `git push` sends your commits to a remote repository (GitHub).
Flow: edit, `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`.
ec:
git add src/App.java
git commit -m "Add user validation"
git push origin feature/validation
r: Edit, add (stage), commit, push.
fa: Working directory, staging area (index), local repository

q: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
o: There is no difference, they do the same thing
`fetch` downloads only; `pull` is fetch plus merge
`pull` uploads your changes; `fetch` deletes them
`fetch` only works for tags, not for branches
e:
`git fetch` updates your knowledge of the remote (new commits and branches) but does not touch your working files. It is safe: you can inspect first (`git log origin/main`).
`git pull` does `fetch` and then merges (or rebases, with `--rebase`) those changes into your current branch immediately. It may cause conflicts you must resolve.
Many people use `git pull --rebase` to keep a linear history.
r: pull = fetch + merge.
fa: `fetch` downloads remote changes without changing your files; `pull` = fetch + merge into your current branch

q: What is the difference between `git reset` and `git revert` for undoing a commit?
o: They are identical in the effect they have on history
`reset` rewrites history; `revert` adds an undoing commit
`revert` deletes the whole repository from the disk
`reset` only works on remote branches, never local
e:
`git reset --hard <commit>` moves your branch pointer back and discards later commits and changes. Fine for local work, but if others already have those commits, you create a mess (it rewrites history).
`git revert <commit>` adds a new commit with the opposite changes. History stays intact, so it is the safe way to undo something already pushed to a shared branch like `main`.
ec:
git revert 3f2a9c1        # safe on shared branches
git reset --hard HEAD~1   # local only: drops last commit and changes
r: Shared branch: revert. Local mess: reset.
fa: `reset` moves the branch back, rewriting history (risky if already pushed); `revert` creates a NEW commit that undoes the old one, safe for shared branches

q: What does `git stash` do?
o: Deletes uncommitted changes forever, with no way back
Saves uncommitted changes on a stack; `stash pop` restores
Pushes the uncommitted changes to the remote branch
Creates a tag on the current commit of the branch
e:
You are halfway through a change and need to switch branch to fix something urgent. You do not want to commit unfinished work.
`git stash` stores your changes in a temporary shelf and gives you a clean directory. Later `git stash pop` reapplies them (and removes them from the shelf); `git stash list` shows the stack.
r: stash = shelf for unfinished work.
fa: Temporarily saves your uncommitted changes on a stack and cleans the working directory, so you can switch tasks; `git stash pop` brings them back

q: What does `git cherry-pick <commit>` do?
o: Deletes a commit from the history of the branch
Applies one commit from another branch onto yours
Merges the entire other branch into your branch
Renames the current branch in the local repository
e:
Sometimes you want just ONE commit from another branch, for example a bug fix made on `develop` that must also go to `release/1.2`.
`git cherry-pick <hash>` copies that commit's changes onto your current branch, creating a new commit with a different hash.
Use it sparingly: duplicated commits can confuse history later.
r: cherry-pick = copy one commit to here.
fa: Applies the changes of one specific commit from another branch onto your current branch as a new commit

q: What is a typical difference between Git Flow and trunk-based development?
o: Git Flow has long-lived branches; trunk-based, short ones
There is no difference between the two in practice
Trunk-based has no branches and also no code review
Git Flow requires no merges at all in the workflow
e:
Git Flow: `main` (releases), `develop` (integration), plus feature, release and hotfix branches. Good for scheduled, versioned releases; heavier process and bigger merges.
Trunk-based development: everyone integrates into `main` very often (at least daily), with small short-lived branches or direct commits, protected by automated tests and feature flags for unfinished work. It fits continuous delivery.
Many teams use a lighter hybrid: feature branch, pull request, merge to main.
r: Git Flow = many long branches. Trunk-based = small, frequent merges to main.
fa: Git Flow uses many long-lived branches (develop, release, hotfix); trunk-based uses short-lived branches merged to `main` frequently, supported by feature flags and CI

q: What is a pull request (PR) / merge request?
o: A request to download Git onto your own machine
A proposal to merge your branch, with review and CI
A backup of the database made before a release
A way to delete a branch from the remote server
e:
After working in your branch, you open a pull request on GitHub/GitLab. It shows the diff, allows comments and approvals (code review), and runs automated checks (build, tests, lint).
Only when reviewers approve and checks pass is the branch merged. This catches bugs early, spreads knowledge and keeps `main` healthy.
Good PRs are small, have a clear description and link to the ticket.
r: PR = review + checks before merging.
fa: A proposal to merge your branch into another, where teammates review the code and CI runs before it is accepted

q: What is the purpose of a `.gitignore` file?
o: To store the access passwords of the repository
To list files Git must not track, like build output
To delete files from the repository automatically
To rename the branches of the repository in bulk
e:
Some files should never be in the repository: compiled output (`target/`, `node_modules/`), IDE folders (`.idea/`), logs, and above all secrets such as `.env` files with passwords.
List patterns in `.gitignore` and Git will not stage them. Note: it does not remove files already tracked; use `git rm --cached file` for those.
If a secret was committed, treat it as leaked: rotate it, since history keeps it.
r: .gitignore keeps build output and secrets out of the repo.
fa: To list files and folders Git should not track (build output like `target/`, IDE settings, secrets, logs)

q: You ran `git reset --hard` by mistake and "lost" commits. What can save you?
o: Nothing; the commits are gone forever after a reset
`git reflog` shows where HEAD was, so you can restore it
Reinstalling Git on the machine you are working on
Deleting the .git folder and cloning the repo again
e:
Git rarely deletes commits immediately. `git reflog` is a local log of every position HEAD has been in (commits, resets, checkouts, rebases).
Find the hash from before the mistake (`HEAD@{3}`) and restore it: `git reset --hard <hash>` or create a branch there: `git branch rescue <hash>`.
Unreferenced commits are kept for roughly 30 to 90 days before garbage collection. Uncommitted changes lost by a hard reset, however, cannot be recovered this way.
ec:
git reflog
git branch rescue HEAD@{2}
r: reflog = Git's undo history for HEAD.
fa: `git reflog` shows where HEAD used to point, so you can find the commit hash and restore it with `git reset` or `git checkout`

q: What are the main phases of the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)?
o: Only coding, because the rest is not part of it
Requirements, design, build, test, deploy, maintain
Marketing, sales, support, and customer success
Compile, link, run, and then package the output
e:
SDLC describes how software goes from idea to production and beyond:
1. Requirements: what must it do and why.
2. Design: architecture, data model, APIs.
3. Implementation: writing code.
4. Testing: unit, integration, acceptance.
5. Deployment: release to users.
6. Maintenance: monitor, fix bugs, improve.
Waterfall does these in strict order; Agile repeats them in short cycles (sprints) with frequent feedback. CI/CD automates testing and deployment.
r: Requirements, design, code, test, deploy, maintain (repeat).
fa: Requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, maintenance

q: What is a good commit message and commit size?
o: 'fix' as the message, and one huge commit per week
A short imperative summary, in a small focused commit
The full source code of the changed file as text
Only emojis as the message, with no further text
e:
Small, focused commits make history readable, reviews easier, `git bisect` possible and reverts safe.
Subject line: imperative mood, about 50 characters ("Add retry to payment client"). Optional body explaining why. Reference the ticket (`PROJ-123`).
Avoid: "fix", "stuff", "WIP", and mixing refactoring with feature changes in one commit.
r: One logical change per commit; explain the why.
fa: A short, imperative summary of WHAT and WHY ("Fix null email in signup"), in a small commit that does one logical change

q: Explain the basic Git workflow you use every day with a team.
a:
- `git switch -c feature/x` (create a branch from an updated `main`).
- Edit, then `git add` and `git commit` small logical commits.
- `git fetch` / `git pull --rebase` to stay up to date with `main`.
- `git push -u origin feature/x`, open a pull request.
- Code review and CI checks; fix feedback with new commits.
- Merge (squash or merge commit, per team rule), delete the branch.
- Resolve conflicts by editing, `git add`, continue; never force-push shared branches.

q: Describe the Maven build lifecycle and how you would fix a dependency conflict.
a:
- Lifecycle: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy; `clean` removes `target/`.
- Dependencies are resolved from Maven Central or a company repository (Nexus/Artifactory) into `~/.m2`.
- Conflict symptoms: `NoSuchMethodError`, `ClassNotFoundException`, two versions of the same library.
- Diagnose with `mvn dependency:tree` (add `-Dverbose`).
- Fix: pin the version in `dependencyManagement`, add `<exclusions>` for the unwanted transitive version, or import a BOM.
- Prevent: use `maven-enforcer-plugin` (dependencyConvergence), avoid SNAPSHOTs in releases.

q: Explain Agile and Scrum to someone who has never worked in a team.
a:
- Agile: build software in small increments, get feedback early, adapt to change; values working software, collaboration and responding to change over rigid plans.
- Scrum is a framework: work in fixed sprints (1 to 4 weeks).
- Roles: Product Owner (decides priorities), Scrum Master (helps the process), Developers.
- Artifacts: product backlog (all wanted work), sprint backlog (chosen for this sprint), increment (working result).
- Events: sprint planning, daily stand-up (15 min), sprint review (demo), retrospective (how to improve).
- Kanban alternative: visual board, limit work in progress, continuous flow.

q: What is version control and why do teams use it?
o: A system that records every change, to compare and undo
Naming the files v1, v2, v3 by hand in a folder
A backup tool that overwrites the previous copy
A code formatter that makes the style consistent
e:
Without version control, people email zip files or end with 'final_v3_REAL.docx'.
With it, every change is recorded with who made it, when and why, and you can go back to any point in history.
Several people can work in parallel and then combine their work (merge).
Git is the most used tool for this.
r: Version control = history + collaboration for code.
fa: A system that records every change to files over time, so you can compare versions, undo mistakes and work together without overwriting each other

q: What is Git?
o: A distributed version control system with full history
A website that hosts the code of many projects
A programming language used for scripting builds
A project management app with boards and tickets
e:
Git was developed in 2005 by the Linux kernel community, led by Linus Torvalds, with goals such as speed, a simple design and strong support for many parallel branches.
'Distributed' means that you have the entire history on your own machine and can work offline.
GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket are services that host Git repositories and add collaboration features. Git and GitHub are not the same thing.
r: Git = the tool. GitHub = a service that hosts Git repos.
fa: A distributed version control system: every developer has a full copy of the project and its history

q: What is a Git repository (repo)?
o: The project folder tracked by Git, with its history
A single commit that was saved in the history
A cloud server that stores the code of a company
A text editor that is used to write the code
e:
GitHub's docs: a repository, or Git project, encompasses the entire collection of files and folders associated with a project, along with each file's revision history.
You get one by running `git init` in a folder, or by copying an existing one with `git clone <url>`.
The local repository and the remote one (for example on GitHub) are separate copies that you synchronize.
r: Repo = project + its full history.
fa: The project folder tracked by Git, with all its files and their history

q: What is a Git commit?
o: A snapshot of your staged changes, with a message
Deleting a file from the project working directory
Sending the code to the production environment
A branch that is created from the current commit
e:
The file history appears as snapshots in time called commits.
You choose what goes in the snapshot with `git add`, then save it with `git commit -m "Fix login error"`. Each commit has an ID, an author, a date and a message.
Good commits are small and have clear messages in the imperative: 'Add', 'Fix', 'Remove'.
r: Commit = a snapshot with a message.
fa: A saved snapshot of your staged changes in the project history, with a message describing it

q: What is a Git branch?
o: A separate line of development, apart from `main`
A copy of the project hosted on another website
A type of commit message with a special format
A file that was deleted from the working directory
e:
Commits can be organized into multiple lines of development called branches.
The usual way to work: create a branch for your feature (`git switch -c feature/login`), commit there, and when it is ready open a pull request to merge it into the main branch.
The main line is often called `main`. Branches are cheap in Git, so use them freely.
r: Branch = a safe parallel line of work.
fa: A separate line of development where you can work without affecting the main line

q: Which sequence is the everyday Git flow to save and share a change?
o: `git add` → `git commit` → `git push`
`git push` → `git add` → `git commit`
`git commit` → `git clone` → `git add`
`git pull` → `git delete`
e:
- `git clone <url>`: copy a remote repo to your machine (once).
- `git add <file>`: choose changes for the next snapshot (staging).
- `git commit -m "message"`: save the snapshot locally.
- `git push`: send your commits to the remote repository.
- `git pull`: bring the others' commits to your machine.
Before starting work, pull; when done, add, commit and push.
r: add → commit → push.

q: What is `pom.xml` in a Maven project?
o: The Project Object Model: dependencies and builds
The main Java class that starts the application
The database script that creates all the tables
A test report that is created after the build
e:
Maven's guide: the pom.xml file is the core of a project's configuration in Maven, a single file with most of the information needed to build the project.
Inside you find the project's coordinates (`groupId`, `artifactId`, `version`), the Java version, and the list of dependencies that Maven downloads for you.
Maven is a build tool, so you describe what you want and it runs the steps.
r: pom.xml = the project's configuration for Maven.
fa: The project's Project Object Model: the main configuration file with its coordinates, dependencies and build settings

q: In a standard Maven project, where do the source code and the test code go?
o: `src/main/java` and `src/test/java`
`bin/main` and `lib/test` folders
`target/src` and `docs/test` folders
`web/java` and `test/java` folders
e:
Maven uses a standard folder layout, so every project looks alike:
- `src/main/java`: your application code.
- `src/test/java`: your tests.
- `src/main/resources`: configuration files such as application.properties.
- `target`: output of the build, like the packaged JAR. You do not edit it and you do not commit it.
r: main code in src/main/java, tests in src/test/java.

q: What does `mvn clean` do?
o: Removes the output of the previous build (`target`)
Deletes your source code from the project folder
Downloads all the dependencies again from the web
Runs the tests of the project in a clean state
e:
Maven has several lifecycles. The `clean` lifecycle removes everything the previous build produced.
A typical command is `mvn clean package`: clean first, then compile, test and package, so old leftovers cannot cause strange results.
For a normal build, the phases run in order: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy.
r: clean = delete previous build output.
fa: Removes files generated by the previous build (the `target` folder)

q: What is a 'build' in software?
o: The automated steps that turn source into a runnable app
Constructing a server room for the engineering team
Writing the very first version of the code of an app
Drawing the UI of an application in a design tool
e:
Source code cannot always be run as it is. A build compiles it, downloads dependencies, runs tests and packages the result (for example a JAR or a Docker image).
Build tools: Maven and Gradle (Java), npm scripts (JavaScript), pip with setuptools or Poetry (Python).
A CI server runs the build on every push, so the team knows right away if it breaks.
r: Build = source code → tested, packaged artifact.
fa: The automated process that turns source code into something that can run or be shipped: compile, run tests, package

q: Explain Git and GitHub to a beginner.
a:
- Git is a tool on your computer that records the history of your project as commits (snapshots).
- It lets you create branches to try changes safely and merge them later.
- GitHub is a website (also GitLab, Bitbucket) that stores a copy of your Git repository online so teams can share it.
- On top of Git, GitHub adds pull requests, code review, issues and automation (Actions).
- Daily flow: clone, create a branch, edit, add, commit, push, open a pull request.
